candidate.answerReason: A nine-keystroke route reaches 200. Any route using at most eight strokes would force 25 to be reached within five strokes, requiring 24 within four, although four strokes can reach at most 16.

methods.label: Bound the displays and force the final steps
methods.explanation:
First, nine keystrokes are possible using the following displays:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1&\to2\to3\to6\to12\\
 &\to24\to25\to50\to100\to200.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each of the nine arrows is either an addition of \(1\) or a doubling. To prove this is the fewest, we must rule out every route using at most eight strokes.

Every display is a positive integer. For a display \(x\ge1\), we have \(x+1\le2x\), so doubling gives the largest possible next display. Repeated doubling therefore bounds the displays after four, five, six, and seven strokes by \(16,32,64,128\), respectively.

Suppose a route reached \(200\) in at most eight strokes. Its final key could not be \([+1]\), because that would require reaching \(199\) in at most seven strokes, exceeding the bound \(128\). Thus it must double \(100\), which must be reached within seven strokes.

Similarly, reaching \(100\) within seven strokes must finish by doubling \(50\), since the alternative predecessor \(99\) exceeds the six-stroke bound \(64\). Reaching \(50\) within six strokes must finish by doubling \(25\), since \(49\) exceeds the five-stroke bound \(32\).

This would reach \(25\) within five strokes. Since \(25\) is odd, its last step must add \(1\) to \(24\). But \(24\) cannot be reached within four strokes, whose maximum is \(16\). This contradiction rules out eight or fewer strokes. The minimum is therefore \(\boxed{9}\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: The proof uses repeated doubling, inverse arithmetic operations, and the fact that doubling an integer produces an even number.
